newsitem.title: INDIA: India panel wants fairplay in insurance reform.
newsitem.headline: India panel wants fairplay in insurance reform.

text.p: A parliamentary committee examining a proposed regulatory law for India's insurance industry said on Friday that reforms in the sector should ensure equal treatment to both state and private firms.

"The committee feel that as and when insurance sector is opened to private sector companies, there should be a level-playing field for all insurance companies whether in the private sector or in the public sector," the committee said in a report presented to parliament.
The standing committee of lawmakers attached to the Finance Ministry was asked to give its views on the Insurance Regulatory Authority Bill, which was introduced in parliament last December.

The bill, if approved, would form a law under which India would set up an insurance regulator to oversee the opening up of a decades-old state monopoly under an economic reform programme launched in 1991.
India began hesitant steps to reform the sector earlier this year when the government said it proposed to allow a few private firms in health insurance.
The insurance sector, in which labour unions are strongly organised, is seen as a major challenge for reformers.
The standing committee recommended that the insurance regulatory body should have five full-time members. Of these, three should have experience in the insurance industry, it said.

"The committee also feels that the members of the Insurance Regulatory Authority on ceasing to be members of the authority should not be permitted to join in companies where insurance funds are deployed," the report said.

Insurance sector reforms have been opposed by leftist political parties who oppose the entry of foreign firms in the industry. New Delhi is under pressure to open up the sector as part of global free trade in services.

In a dissenting note to the standing committee's report, one of its members, Biplab Dasgupta of the Communist Party of India-Marxist(CPI-M), said he was in total disagreement with the Insurance Regulatory Authority Bill.
"This bill can make sense only in the context of liberalisation extending to free entry of the foreign multinationals entering the Indian economy," he said.
The CPI-M is one of the constituents of India's ruling centre-left coalition, the United Front. But it is not represented in Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's ministry.
